shelfmark: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College, MS 173 (the ‘Parker Manuscript’)
wormald_date: Laws written in the 930s, by two scribes, at about the time they were joined to the Chronicle: after quires 1–3 of the Chronicle (to ‘924’) were finished (palaeographically not after 930) and before quire 4 (annals from ‘925’) was added, probably in the 950s, perhaps before 951 (p. 166). Table 4.1: s. x^med (p. 164). The book was copied (into Otho B.xi) in the early eleventh century (pp. 163, 180).
wormald_origin: Most probably Winchester by the mid-tenth century (Winchester-centred episcopal data, marks for Ealhswith’s death and Frithestan’s accession), though Dumville’s doubts are acknowledged and a court origin is as possible as a royal abbey; Wormald thinks it does not greatly matter which (pp. 167–71). At Christ Church Canterbury by the later eleventh century and continued there (pp. 167, 180); possibly taken there by Ælfheah on his move from Winchester in 1006, after having it copied (p. 180). Table 4.1: Winchester (s. x^med)/Canterbury (after 1001) (p. 164). Wormald argues these books belonged to bishops (p. 181).
laws: Af–Ine (the combined law-book of Alfred and Ine), ff. 33r–52v (p. 163). Text heavily corrupt: e.g. a line lost by eye-skip at Af 1:2; ‘ceape’ for ‘ceace’ at Ine 37 and 62 (with Ine Rb. 62); Af 8 ‘munuc’ for ‘nunnan’ (pp. 171–2 and nn. 38–40).
laws_liebermann: Af, Ine
other_contents: Mainly the Parker (A) text of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, kept up from the early 890s to the late eleventh century (to 1093 as the book now stands), preceding the laws; after the laws, papal and episcopal lists and Sedulius’ Carmen Paschale (some damaged leaves restored in a hand very like Chronicle scribe 1’s; perhaps joined to the book only c. 1600). The laws form a self-contained two-quire ‘booklet’ in two hands found nowhere else, but quire signatures show they were once the collection’s fourth and fifth quires, directly after Chronicle quires 1–3 (pp. 163–6).
overview: The Parker Manuscript is above all the oldest Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, and its copy of the Alfred–Ine law-book, made in the 930s by two scribes, was deliberately added to the Chronicle as a continuation of it, as quire signatures and matching page layout show. It was probably at Winchester in the mid-tenth century, close to the West Saxon court, and had reached Christ Church, Canterbury, before the end of the eleventh century. The legal text is far from accurate, and the book's interest is historical rather than practical: it placed West Saxon law alongside the annals of West Saxon military success.
liebermann_superseded: Liebermann held that the laws had no original connection with the Chronicle before or after them; Wormald accepts that the booklets had lives of their own but shows from quire signatures and matching page format that the law quires were joined to the Chronicle soon after they were written, in the 930s (p. 166).
key_quote: “the Parker laws were copied by and for people deeply implicated in the West Saxon dynasty’s audacious attempt to persuade the English at large” (p. 171)
doubts: GUIDE: the guide (Liebermann) says the laws are in one hand of c. 925; Wormald (p. 163) says two hands, and dates them to the 930s (p. 166, ‘best assigned to the 930s’, checked in image). The guide’s ‘not the exemplar of the others’ needs care: Wormald notes (p. 174 and n. 44) that Liebermann himself thought the Otho Alfred–Ine copied from E, and Wormald agrees (pp. 173–5). Wormald cites Ker, Catalogue no. 39, and Gesetze I p. xxiv. Table 4.1 date s. x^med checked in image. In the early eleventh century the lists preceded the laws, and by 1600 the Sedulius did (pp. 163–6).

wormald_heading: 1 (ii) BL, Cotton MS Otho B.xi + BL, Additional MS 43703
shelfmark: London, British Library, Cotton MS Otho B.xi (with the detached king-list leaf now BL, Additional MS 34652, f. 2)
wormald_date: Bede mid-tenth century; main assemblage (Chronicle, lists, law-book and the rest) 1001×1012, since the Chronicle ends at 1001 and the episcopal lists were extended by another hand to 1012×1013; the Æthelstan code in a third hand possibly of the time of those additions (pp. 172–3). Table 4.1: 1001x1015 (p. 164).
wormald_origin: Winchester: the Bede scribe also wrote the Parker annals ‘925’–946/55, and the Chronicle, lists and law-book were probably copied from the Parker MS (p. 173; Table 4.1, p. 164); copied soon after 1001, perhaps for Ælfheah’s successor at Winchester when Ælfheah took the Parker MS to Canterbury in 1006 — a guess Wormald flags as unsupported (p. 180). Wanley says it came from St Mary’s Southwick (p. 180 n. 75). Badly damaged in the Cotton fire (p. 173); its last items destroyed in 1731 (p. 178). Basis of Whelock’s editio princeps of the Chronicle (p. 174, n. 42 cont.). Wormald argues episcopal, not lay, ownership (p. 181).

Af–Ine, copied from the Parker MS but with the line lost at Af 1:2 restored (probably by correction) (pp. 174–5). Ymb Æwbricas, a short text on adultery added straight after Ine’s last law (pp. 175–6). Only two leaves of II As and three of Af–Ine survive (p. 173). V As and Iudex were NOT in Otho (p. 176).
laws_liebermann: Af, Ine, II As
other_contents: Old English Bede (mid-tenth century), completed by the main scribe with Bede’s autobiographical ending; Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (G for Chronicle editors, Plummer’s A) to 1001 with prefatory West Saxon genealogical king-list (leaf now Add. 34652, f. 2); papal and episcopal lists; then, after the laws, the Burghal Hidage, the poem ‘Seasons of Fasting’, and medical recipes (mostly also in Bald’s Leechbook, a book written by the scribe of the Parker ‘925’ annals and the Otho Bede). Once 231 leaves; under a quarter survive. The lost parts are known from Nowell’s transcript (Add. 43703) and Wanley’s description and annotations (Bodleian, Gough London 54) (pp. 172–80).
overview: A Winchester compilation of 1001×1012 in which a mid-tenth-century Old English Bede was continued with a Chronicle, lists and Alfred and Ine's laws probably all copied from the Parker Manuscript (plus an added text on adultery), the Burghal Hidage, verses on the fasts and medical recipes; a third scribe squeezed in a variant text of Æthelstan’s Grately code. Largely burnt in 1731, it is known chiefly from Laurence Nowell’s transcript of 1562 and Wanley’s description. Wormald sees the whole as essentially a historical collection about the English people, probably made in an episcopal setting.
liebermann_superseded: Liebermann knew Otho only from its burnt fragments (Af–Ine and II As 7–25); Nowell’s 1562 transcript, unknown to him, shows the original held a complete variant Grately code, an added text on adultery (Ymb Æwbricas), the Burghal Hidage and other items (pp. 173–8).

overview: Laurence Nowell's 1562 transcript of almost the whole of Otho B.xi, later corrected and glossed by him, is the main witness to the contents of that manuscript before the 1731 fire, including texts known from nowhere else. At the end Nowell added the Exeter code of Æthelstan (V As), Iudex and the close of the Grately code — texts he took from another manuscript, now lost.

wormald_origin: Worcester (Table 4.1, p. 164; argued cumulatively pp. 184–5). The two leaves once belonged to a fairly imposing (probably liturgical) book (pp. 182–3); possibly incorporated early in the eleventh-century Worcester cathedral cartulary, which was probably bound into one of the sister-Bibles of the Codex Amiatinus at Worcester (perhaps the ‘Offa Bible’) (p. 184). laws_liebermann: IV Eg
other_contents: The two leaves: on f. 185r an incomplete liturgical text (excerpts from Bede's commentary on Mark alternating with responses found as lections for a martyr in a thirteenth-century Worcester antiphonary), first line erased. The host volume (Nero E.i, vol. II) as listed by Cotton: last 155 leaves of part I of the Worcester legendary ('Passional', whose second part is in the Parker Library); twelfth-century Lives of Frideswide, David and Margaret; fifteen leaves of part II of the legendary (ff. 166–80); four leaves of an eleventh-century Worcester cathedral cartulary (ff. 181–4); the law leaves; two leaves of a Life of Bede (ff. 187–8, reversed); thirty-four thirteenth-century leaves of vitae and passiones (ff. 189–222) (p. 183).
overview: Two large leaves (the largest of all the surviving law manuscripts) carrying a complete copy of IV Edgar, written about the turn of the tenth and eleventh centuries: the second-oldest extant law manuscript and, apart from three Wulfstan books, the copy nearest in date to the code. The pages were ruled for two columns and seem to come from a substantial liturgical volume; a later scribe added a liturgical text on the preceding page. Wormald suggests that they were kept from an early date within the Worcester cathedral cartulary (itself probably bound into a great Bible), and thinks their Worcester provenance all but certain even though the code concerns the Danelaw; Oswald, bishop of Worcester and archbishop of York, may explain its presence there.
liebermann_superseded: Liebermann dated the leaves c. 1030 and called them unrelated to the cartulary leaves beside them; Wormald follows Ker’s date of s. x/xi, making it the second-oldest surviving law manuscript, and suggests the leaves may have been lodged in the Worcester cartulary from an early date (pp. 182–4).

overview: The first four leaves of Harley 55 are an early eleventh-century fragment, once the end of a larger book, holding a medical tract, a copy of II–III Edgar and Archbishop Oswald's list of estates lost by York. The code and the memorandum carry corrections and additions in the hand Ker identified as Archbishop Wulfstan's, so this is the earliest of the law-books to show Wulfstan's own intervention; its text of Edgar shares several substantive additions with other Wulfstan manuscripts and alone has a clause on Friday fasting. It was at York or Worcester (certainly at Worcester in the thirteenth century), and there is no clear sign of its association with the mid-twelfth-century Cnut quire (Part B) until the later sixteenth century; Selden may have joined them.

overview: The second, older part of Cotton Nero A.i is a small, pocket-sized collection of Wulfstan's writings from his own lifetime, corrected and glossed in the archbishop's own hand: homilies, the Institutes of Polity and laws (I Æthelstan, I Edmund and II–III Edgar, much of them now lost with a missing bifolium, two differing copies of V Æthelred, Grið, the opening of VIII Æthelred and Norðgrið), followed by a Latin canon-law collection that fed his Old English writings. Wormald dates it to the beginning of the eleventh century and thinks its quires may come from two or more closely similar Wulfstan books rather than one planned volume; it was probably joined to the later legal part A only in the sixteenth century. Its mix of law, homily and Polity suggests a moral handbook for a travelling preacher rather than a judge's manual, and its origin (Worcester or York) cannot be settled beyond Wulfstan's own circle.

overview: Corpus 201 is a tall, narrow mid-eleventh-century book, most probably assembled at the New Minster, Winchester, by several scribes who built on an unfinished collection of devotional texts begun half a century earlier. That collection seems to have been shaped at York, where the Northumbrian Priests' Law was added, before reaching Winchester, where the book may have served to train future monk-bishops in both pastoral and governmental duties.
